overview: This card follows Cambodia’s royal society after Angkor through the early French protectorate. The atlas uses 1492-1878, not the kingdom’s foundation and extinction dates. Its earlier outline reaches far into the Mekong delta and cuts off much of the north; later outlines expand northward. These repeated shapes simplify changing royal power and regional influence. Angkor’s continuing religious life provides related northern context even when the site falls outside the displayed outline. The earlier Khmer Empire and modern Cambodia have separate map records.

periods.title: Longvek and international commerce
periods.summary: Longvek became a major sixteenth-century royal and trading center. Archaeology complements much later royal chronicles.

periods.title: War, rebuilding and shifting courts
periods.summary: Ayutthaya’s capture of Longvek changed politics, but exchange continued. Oudong became a major royal center; expanding neighboring powers altered access to trade.

periods.title: Royal diplomacy under pressure
periods.summary: Siamese and Vietnamese influence constrained Cambodia. King Ang Duong explored French diplomatic ties before Norodom’s protectorate treaty.

periods.title: The early French protectorate
periods.summary: The 1863 treaty changed external authority while the Cambodian monarchy continued. The atlas stops in 1878, before further colonial intervention.

items.text: Longvek stood beside the Tonle Sap River, linking the court with routes toward the Mekong delta. The roughly seven-square-kilometer fortified area supported religious, political and commercial activity. Later chronicles connect its rise with King Ang Chan I around 1530; excavated objects provide evidence independent of that remembered royal story.

Longvek’s defenses worked with the landscape. Surveyors recorded clay embankments and moats, with three lines on the north and west and one on the south. The eastern side opened toward the river floodplain. Building a royal city required understanding seasonal water as well as preparing for armies.

A 2019 study chemically analyzed 102 brown-glazed storage-jar fragments and distinguished seven compositional groups. Comparisons connected parts of the assemblage with production in Thailand, southern China and Cambodia. Chemistry helps researchers follow containers across seas even when a broken jar has lost its label, handles or recognizable shape.

Storage jars carried food and other commodities and could remain useful for generations. Some older Cambodian jars were still circulating during Longvek’s early modern occupation. A sturdy container did not need replacing just because a new king arrived. Reuse also makes a vessel’s manufacture date different from the date it was discarded.

Among high-value finds from Longvek’s central mound, a white porcelain fragment appears to come from a frog-shaped container. Other imported dishes used green, yellow and purple glazes. Researchers associate these unusual luxuries with courtly or high-ranking households. The little ceramic frog was probably closer to a prized possession than everyone’s everyday bowl.

The capture of Longvek by Ayutthaya in 1594 disrupted royal institutions, but imported ceramics show trade continuing afterward. The city’s occupation did not end in one dramatic afternoon. Later struggles over the delta’s outlets and customs revenues changed the commercial setting, while royal activity shifted toward Oudong and nearby centers.

A 2024 study of animal remains from Longvek’s palace area identified pig, cattle, deer and serow, a goat-like animal. Cut marks on some cattle bones show butchery. These scraps reveal practical food preparation, although the palace also contained workers and dependents: the bones cannot tell us which meals belonged to kings.

Rubbish pits beside the palace contained animal bones and pottery; burning and cut marks helped identify a food-preparation context. Even kitchen waste can become a historical archive. The study also warns that excavation methods probably missed many small fish bones, so big animal bones should not be mistaken for the whole menu.

An Angkor Wat inscription from 1663 records a woman’s religious gifts and the freeing of an enslaved man. Her husband, seriously ill, had requested his release and a gift of silver; relatives and named witnesses supported the decision. This unusually personal record preserves a household’s relationships within a society where slavery existed.

The same inscription describes Buddhist images commissioned in gold and silver and the invitation of thirty monks for recitations. Food was offered to them the following morning. A donation brought together patrons, religious specialists and witnesses, leaving an enduring written trace of activities that otherwise might disappear with a single gathering.

A surviving palm-leaf manuscript intended for young people contains a Khmer didactic treatise, ending with Pali phrases and Khmer translations. The British Library dates this copy to the eighteenth or early nineteenth century. Its eight leaves carry five lines on each surface. Learning could involve a carefully handled bundle of leaves rather than a bound schoolbook.

Another manuscript, dated 1830, preserves a love poem in yellow ink on black paper. Its 54 folds make a long concertina book. The contrast would have made the words stand out beautifully when unfolded. Surviving books therefore preserve affection and literary enjoyment alongside the religious and moral works that fill many collections.

sections.title: A written word and changing authority

items.text: A small Middle Khmer writing sample is prabandh, meaning “wife,” in the 1663 inscription’s reference to Hiem. This is the scholarly Roman-letter transcription of the historical Khmer word, not a photograph or a reconstruction of its carved letters. The editor explains its spelling while translating the husband’s instructions to his wife.

Angkor remained a place of worship after royal power moved elsewhere. An 1866 photograph by Émile Gsell shows a thatched monastic dwelling beside Angkor Wat’s western causeway. Monks and pilgrims kept using the site. Calling it a lost city discovered by Europeans would erase the people who had continued to care for it.

Ang Duong sought diplomatic contact with France, but Siamese pressure obstructed a mission in 1856. Norodom concluded the protectorate treaty in August 1863. A French resident and resource concessions changed the balance of power. In 1867, France recognized Siam’s control of Battambang and Siem Reap in return for Siam relinquishing claims over the rest of Cambodia.

ending.text: The 1863 protectorate changed Cambodia’s external political position without abolishing its monarchy or ending Khmer cultural life. The 1878 map cutoff marks neither a final conquest nor independence. French intervention deepened afterward, so this early protectorate phase belongs within a longer colonial transformation.
